overview.title: Reading Skala-Podilska through its memorial book
overview.summary: Skala-Podilska was a Jewish town in southeastern Galicia on the Zbruch River, shaped by religious tradition, commerce, education, cultural activity, and changing imperial and national regimes. The memorial book follows this community from its earlier history and vibrant interwar institutions through Soviet rule, Nazi occupation, deportation, murder, flight, hiding, and partisan resistance. It also preserves the voices of survivors and descendants who rebuilt lives elsewhere and created memorials, ceremonies, and the 1978 Yizkor book. These paths help readers understand both what was destroyed and how Skala’s people, traditions, and memories endured.

paths.title: What kind of Jewish community was Skala?
paths.description: Explore how geography, religion, work, family life, education, and culture made Skala a living community rather than merely a wartime location. By the end, you will see the institutions and relationships that gave Skala its distinctive character.
paths.question: How did Jewish life function in Skala before the Holocaust?

steps.title: A border-town community
steps.summary: The memorial book places Skala in southeastern Galicia on the Zbruch River and describes it as a border town with smugglers, carters, and porters. steps.summary: The book remembers Skala as a Hasidic town with several Hasidic groups and religious leaders, including the rabbinic Drimer and Laufer families. paths.title: How did political change affect Skala?
paths.description: Follow Skala through the First World War, Polish and Soviet rule, Zionist organizing, and the arrival of German occupation. You will understand how state power repeatedly altered ordinary community life before the destruction began.
paths.question: What did changing governments mean for Skala’s Jews?

paths.title: How was Skala’s Jewish population destroyed?
paths.description: Trace the escalating system of forced labor, deportation, ghettos, camps, shootings, and Aktionen described in the memorial book. The path shows how destruction unfolded over time and affected both the community as a whole and named individuals.
paths.question: How did persecution become mass murder?

paths.title: How did people survive, resist, and help one another?
paths.description: Read survivor accounts of flight, hiding, underground bunkers, escape routes, mutual aid, and armed resistance. By the end, you will see survival as a series of dangerous choices made by individuals and groups, not as a single outcome.
paths.question: What forms did survival and resistance take?

steps.title: Aid and escape routes
steps.summary: Skala Jews provided food, clothing, medical care, and transport assistance to deportees passing through the town. Three young survivors later reached Skala and obtained documents to cross into Hungary, showing how local help could create a route to safety. paths.title: What survived after Skala was destroyed?
paths.description: Follow survivors after liberation as they returned, emigrated, pursued justice, supported one another, and built memorial practices. You will understand how the community continued through people, institutions, testimony, and organized remembrance.
paths.question: How did Skala’s survivors carry the community forward?

steps.title: Liberation and the few survivors
steps.summary: The Red Army liberated Skala at the end of March 1944, but the memorial book emphasizes that only a few Jews survived. Survivors’ accounts, including Shalom Grinberg’s testimony, became essential records of families and events that had been destroyed. steps.title: The Yizkor book as memorial work
steps.summary: At a New York Yizkor gathering in November 1960, participants approved preparing a Skala memorial book, and the initiative began in 1961 after years of effort in America and Israel. The 1978 book therefore preserves not only wartime testimony but also the survivors’ determination to restore Skala’s people, places, and public life to memory. timeline.title: Skala under changing imperial rule
timeline.summary: The memorial book describes the 1772 partition of Poland and later Jewish efforts to gain civil rights after the upheavals of 1848. It presents these changes as part of the political and social setting in which Skala’s Jewish community developed. timeline.dateLabel: First World War and its aftermath
timeline.title: Occupation, exile, and return
timeline.summary: Russian forces occupied Skala in August 1914, and Jewish residents fled or were expelled during the war. Afterward, residents returned and rebuilt institutions, while the area was again captured by the Red Army in 1920. timeline.title: Soviet annexation and expulsions
timeline.summary: Skala was annexed to the Soviet Union in September 1939. Soviet authorities closed the People’s Library, arrested individuals, expelled 17 Jewish families, and sent prisoners’ family members and other Jewish families to Siberia. timeline.title: Ghettos, forests, and resistance

The Ashendorf Youth Band, founded in the ghetto, operated as a Jewish partisan unit in Tsiganer Forest. timeline.title: Liberation of Skala
timeline.summary: The Red Army liberated Skala at the end of March 1944, but the memorial book emphasizes that only a few Jews survived. Accounts of massacres and bunker killings explain why liberation did not mean the restoration of the prewar community.
